routes.label: Use divisibility of the running totals

question: Mrs. Walter gave an exam in a mathematics class of five students. She entered the scores in random order into a spreadsheet, which recalculated the class average after each score was entered. Mrs. Walter noticed that after each score was entered, the average was always an integer. The scores (listed in ascending order) were \(71,\) \(76,\) \(80,\) \(82,\) and \(91.\) What was the last score Mrs. Walter entered?
solution:
After \(k\) scores have been entered, their average is an integer exactly when their sum is divisible by \(k\). This lets us work backward from the total
\[
71+76+80+82+91=400.
\]
Let \(L\) be the last score entered. The first four scores sum to \(400-L\), which must be divisible by \(4\). Since \(400\) is divisible by \(4\), so is \(L\). Among the given scores, only \(76\) and \(80\) satisfy this condition.

Suppose \(76\) were last. The first four scores would then sum to \(324\). Removing the fourth score must leave a first-three total divisible by \(3\). Because \(324\) is itself divisible by \(3\), the fourth score would also have to be divisible by \(3\). But none of the available scores \(71,80,82,91\) is divisible by \(3\). Thus \(76\) cannot be last.

To verify that \(80\) can be last, use the order
\[
76,82,91,71,80.
\]
The successive averages are
\[
76,\quad\frac{158}{2}=79,\quad
\frac{249}{3}=83,\quad
\frac{320}{4}=80,\quad
\frac{400}{5}=80.
\]
All are integers. Therefore the last score was \(\boxed{80}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
